summary: Specifies Geneve, a generic encapsulation for network virtualization. Tunnel needs vary because the devices involved, such as software and hardware tunnel endpoints and central control, differ widely, so Geneve is designed to be flexible and extensible. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Virtual networks need to wrap their messages in an outer envelope to travel across a real network. Geneve is a flexible envelope design that works for many different kinds of equipment.

questions: how big is the geneve header
subtitle: A flexible tunnel header with room for extensible metadata, built to carry virtual networks across ordinary IP data center fabrics.

tldr.problem: Network virtualization needs tunnels that can carry more metadata than a 24-bit identifier and that keep up with changing control planes, hypervisor switches, hardware and middleboxes.
tldr.mechanism: Geneve wraps the original packet in UDP over IPv4 or IPv6, behind a small fixed 8-byte header that carries a 24-bit Virtual Network Identifier, followed by optional Type-Length-Value options that tunnel endpoints define and interpret.
tldr.outcome: Geneve is a Proposed Standard that defines only the data plane and leaves the control plane open, so it can replace or coexist with VXLAN and NVGRE. Its security rests on isolating the underlay or adding IPsec-style protection.

today: RFC 8926 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the specification of Geneve. It sits alongside the earlier VXLAN and NVGRE encapsulations, which the RFC expects Geneve to coexist with during any transition.

sections.title: Why Another Encapsulation
sections.content:
Geneve (Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation) is a tunneling protocol for network virtualization. Many encapsulations already exist, from VLANs and MPLS to VXLAN (RFC 7348) and NVGRE (RFC 7637). The RFC argues that network virtualization is different: it treats the IP network as the backplane of a distributed system, much like a chassis switch, with tunnel endpoints at the edge acting as line cards.

That view needs more metadata than a tenant identifier. Most virtualization protocols have a 24-bit identifier, which the RFC says starts to look small next to the tags used inside a chassis switch. Metadata can range from input port identifiers for simple security policies to service context for middleboxes that terminate and re-encapsulate Geneve traffic.

Rather than prescribe a whole system, Geneve provides a framework for tunneling. It describes the data format and says little about how a control plane decides what to put in it.
sections.eli5: Older envelopes only had room for one little label. Geneve adds space for more notes, because the people sending virtual mail want to attach all sorts of information.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
Geneve targets data center environments, where tunnels act as a backplane between virtual switches in hypervisors, physical switches and middleboxes. Any IP network can be the underlay, though Clos networks that use ECMP (equal cost multipath) links are a common choice. The RFC sets three requirements: a data plane generic enough for current and future control planes, tunnel components that are efficient in both hardware and software, and high performance over existing IP fabrics.

Control plane independence. VXLAN prescribed a multicast-learning control plane, yet its packet format has seen a wide variety of control planes built on top. Geneve is a pure tunnel format specification and explicitly selects no control plane.

Data plane extensibility. Options let new metadata types be defined, deployed and later finalized or retired. They are useful in data packets as well as control packets, so the RFC does not restrict them to control traffic. Options use the Type-Length-Value format.

Standard IP fabrics. Fabrics spread load by hashing addresses and port numbers, and a tunnel hides the inner flow. So entropy from the encapsulated packet must be exposed in the tunnel header, most commonly through the UDP source port.

Tunnel endpoints must parse the variable-length header and act on it. Transit devices (routers and switches along the path) MUST NOT modify Geneve headers and MUST NOT insert or delete options. Interpreting options is OPTIONAL for them.
sections.eli5: The envelope must work with any post office, not just one. Mail sorters only look at the outside, so the outside needs a hint about which truck to use to spread the load.

sections.title: Packet Layout and the UDP Header
sections.content:
A Geneve packet is a compact tunnel header carried in UDP over IPv4 or IPv6. The tunnel header is followed by variable-length options, and then the payload, which is a protocol data unit of the indicated type such as an Ethernet frame. The RFC's examples show the whole stack over Ethernet: outer Ethernet, outer IP, outer UDP, Geneve header, then the inner frame. The original frame's preamble, start frame delimiter and frame check sequence are not included.

The outer UDP header is used as follows:

  • Source port: chosen by the originating tunnel endpoint. It SHOULD be the same for all packets of one encapsulated flow, to avoid reordering, and SHOULD come from a hash of the encapsulated headers such as a 5-tuple. The full 16-bit range MAY be used. With IPv6 the flow label MAY also supply entropy.
  • Destination port: IANA assigned port 6081. Implementations SHOULD make it configurable (RECOMMENDED), and it MUST NOT be reversed for the two ends of a connection as TCP does.
  • Checksum: SHOULD be generated over IPv4. Over IPv6 it MUST be generated by default, and receivers that see a non-zero checksum MUST validate it and drop the packet if it is wrong.
sections.eli5: The Geneve envelope rides inside a normal UDP envelope. The sender picks the return-address number cleverly, so routers sort packets from different conversations onto different roads.

sections.title: The Geneve Header Fields
sections.content:
The fixed header is 8 bytes. Its fields are:

  • Ver (2 bits): the current version is 0. Tunnel endpoints MUST drop packets with an unknown version. Transit devices treat them as UDP packets with an unknown payload.
  • Opt Len (6 bits): length of the options in 4-byte multiples, excluding the 8-byte fixed header. Total header size is therefore from 8 to 260 bytes. Transit devices MUST forward consistently whatever the value, including for ECMP link selection.
  • O (1 bit): control packet. Tunnel endpoints MUST NOT forward its payload, and transit devices MUST NOT interpret it.
  • C (1 bit): critical options present. If set, endpoints MUST parse the options, and endpoints that cannot parse options MUST drop the packet. Transit devices MUST NOT drop packets because of this bit.
  • Protocol Type (16 bits): follows the Ethertype convention, and Ethernet is 0x6558.
  • VNI (24 bits): identifies a unique element of a virtual network, often an L2 segment. The control plane defines the forwarding meaning, and the VNI MAY feed ECMP decisions.
  • Two reserved fields (6 and 8 bits) MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: The header is a short form: a version number, how long the extra notes are, a flag for special messages, a flag for must-read notes, what kind of mail is inside, and the number of the virtual network it belongs to.

sections.title: Tunnel Options
sections.content:
After the base header come zero or more options in Type-Length-Value format. Each has a 4-byte option header followed by option data. The header holds a 16-bit Option Class (a namespace for the type, so each organization can allocate types on its own), an 8-bit Type, three reserved bits and a 5-bit Length in 4-byte multiples that excludes the option header. A single option is therefore between 4 and 128 bytes.

The high-order bit of the Type marks a critical option. A receiving tunnel endpoint that does not recognize a critical option MUST drop the packet, and if any option has the bit set, the C bit in the base header MUST also be set. Transit devices MUST NOT drop packets over unknown options, even critical ones, and MUST NOT modify the options or their order. If the total of the option lengths does not equal Opt Len, the packet is invalid and MUST be silently dropped by an endpoint that processes options. An endpoint whose options capacity is exceeded by Opt Len MUST also drop the packet.

Options are meant to be self-descriptive and independent, which allows parallel processing. An option defined with a fixed length MUST NOT be redefined to a different length. A new Type should be allocated instead.
sections.eli5: Each extra note says whose note it is, what kind it is and how long it is. If a note is marked must-read and the receiver cannot read it, the receiver throws the whole envelope away. The mail carriers in between never touch the notes.

sections.title: Deployment and Operation
sections.content:
Geneve is intended for public or private data centers run by a single operator or a set of cooperating operators, which fit the RFC 8085 idea of a controlled environment. It has no native congestion control, so it MUST be used with congestion-controlled traffic or inside a traffic-managed controlled environment (TMCE) where the operator avoids congestion by provisioning, rate limiting and traffic engineering.

Zero UDP checksum. Over IPv4 an operator MAY set a zero checksum if integrity comes from elsewhere, such as IPsec. Over IPv6 the checksum MUST be on by default. A zero checksum is allowed only in a TMCE and when corruption is very unlikely, measured to be tolerably low, or the payload tolerates corruption. It must also meet the requirements of RFC 6936, and receivers SHOULD check source and destination addresses.

Fragmentation, DSCP, ECN and TTL. Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191, RFC 8201) is RECOMMENDED, and the maximum option length MUST be assumed when computing the tunnel MTU. DSCP follows the Pipe model of RFC 2983 more naturally than the Uniform model. ECN handling per RFC 6040 MUST be followed, and the TTL treatment of RFC 2003 is RECOMMENDED.

Other points. Tunnels may be unicast or use broadcast or multicast, and multicast can be replicated over unicast tunnels. A Geneve tunnel is generally a unidirectional concept. A control plane may limit the number, order and size of options. For NIC offloads, LSO MUST replicate the whole Geneve header and all options onto each segment, and options MUST NOT be reordered. NICs MUST NOT drop packets with unknown options unless configured to. Inner VLAN handling is OPTIONAL and set by configuration.

For transition, Geneve looks like plain UDP to most devices, so it can coexist with VXLAN and NVGRE, and implementations are strongly suggested to run both at once.
sections.eli5: Geneve is meant for one company's own roads, where the company can keep traffic jams away. It needs sensible choices about checksums, big packets and special hardware, and it can happily share the road with older envelope styles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Geneve has no inherent security mechanisms. An attacker on the underlay can snoop on, alter or inject packets, and compromised endpoints or transit devices can spoof header identifiers to reach other tenants' networks. Within a single security domain the most common defense is isolating trusted components, for example carrying tunnel traffic on a separate VLAN and filtering at untrusted boundaries. Across untrusted links, VPN technologies such as IPsec (RFC 4301) should protect the packets.

  • Confidentiality: if the operator decides it is needed, an encryption mechanism SHOULD be used end to end between tunnel endpoints, for example IPsec or DTLS. Overlay data leaving the operator's security domain SHOULD be encrypted.
  • Integrity: an NVE MUST NOT propagate Geneve packets to tenant systems and MUST NOT interpret tenant packets as anything other than frames to encapsulate. Where tampering is a risk, a data integrity mechanism SHOULD be used.
  • Peer authentication: operators SHOULD authenticate peers, for example with IPsec, where spoofing is a threat.
  • Transit devices: where they interpret options, the operator MUST ensure they are trusted.

Protection of control plane traffic is left out of scope.
sections.eli5: The envelope has no lock. If the road is not trusted, you need to put it in a locked box (like IPsec), and make sure nobody inside the building can pretend to be someone else.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated UDP port 6081, with the service name geneve, as the well-known destination port for Geneve. IANA also created a new registry called Geneve Option Class under a new Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO3) heading. It holds 16-bit values with descriptions, assignee and contact information, and references.

The registration rules split the space into three ranges: 0x0000-0x00FF by IETF Review, 0x0100-0xFEFF First Come First Served, and 0xFF00-0xFFFF for Experimental Use.
sections.eli5: Geneve got its own mailbox number, 6081, and a public notebook where companies can sign up for their own sets of note types.
